summary: Specifies two solutions for on-path telemetry of multicast traffic using IOAM, based on the trace option and the direct export option. They support correlating telemetry data and rebuilding the multicast tree without redundant data.

eli5.summary: When one message is copied to many receivers, you want to follow all its trips. This shows how to collect travel notes from every copy.

questions: what is a multicast branch id
how to reconstruct a multicast tree with ioam
subtitle: How to collect IOAM telemetry from multicast traffic without repeating the same data on every branch.

tldr.problem: Multicast packets are copied at each branch of a tree. IOAM trace data then gets duplicated in every copy, while postcard-style export (IOAM DEX) loses track of which branch a postcard came from.
tldr.mechanism: One solution adds a Multicast Branch ID (a Branching Node ID plus an Interface Index) to the IOAM DEX header. The other exports the trace gathered so far as a postcard at every branch fork node and then resets the trace.
tldr.outcome: A collector can rebuild the multicast tree and measure delay, jitter and drops without redundant data. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and registers two new IOAM DEX Extension-Flags.

today: RFC 9630 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2024 and has not been obsoleted or updated. IANA has registered the two IOAM DEX Extension-Flags it defines.

sections.title: Why Multicast Needs Its Own Telemetry
sections.content:
IP multicast carries real-time traffic such as interactive meetings, IPTV and financial market data, all of which rely on UDP's unreliable transport. A single lost packet inside a video keyframe can leave many receivers unable to decode later frames, so the RFC treats monitoring multicast performance as essential.

Newer on-path telemetry such as IOAM (RFC 9197) and IOAM Direct Export (DEX, RFC 9326) works well for unicast, but multicast traffic makes it awkward. The RFC lays out two solutions based on the IOAM trace option and the DEX option. It does not cover operational questions such as enabling telemetry on only a subset of traffic.
sections.eli5: Many people watch the same live show, so one lost piece can spoil it for lots of them. We need a good way to check how every copy of the show travelled.

sections.title: What Multicast Telemetry Must Achieve
sections.content:
Multicast traffic follows a tree built by a routing protocol such as PIM (RFC 7761) or Point-to-Multipoint (P2MP). The solutions in this RFC address three requirements:

  • Reconstruct and visualize the multicast tree through data-plane monitoring.
  • Gather multicast packet delay and jitter on each path.
  • Find where multicast packets are dropped, and why.

Conventional OAM tools such as multicast ping (RFC 6450), mtrace (RFC 8487) and RTCP (RFC 3605) are not enough to meet all three, because the data must be derived from the multicast packets themselves.
sections.eli5: We want to draw the map of who got which copy, see how long each trip took, and find where copies went missing.

sections.title: Problems With Existing Techniques
sections.content:
A multicast packet is replicated at each branch fork node, so several copies exist in the network. This breaks both main IOAM styles.

With the IOAM trace option, the partial trace data is copied into every branch. By the time packets reach the leaves, each copy carries a full trace, and most of that data is repeated across copies when only one copy is needed. The bigger the tree, the worse the overhead and wasted bandwidth.

With postcard-based methods such as IOAM DEX, each node sends a postcard holding only local data, so nothing is duplicated. But postcards carry no branching information. If Node B has branches to Node C and Node D, a collector cannot tell from postcards alone whether Node E follows C or D, unless it correlates with tree knowledge gathered another way, which the RFC calls undesirable extra work. The root cause is that there is no identifier, implicit or explicit, to correlate data on each branch.
sections.eli5: Either every copy of the note-pad is full of the same old notes, or the notes come in without saying which road they belong to. Both are a mess.

sections.title: Solution One: Per-Hop Postcard With a Branch ID
sections.content:
The first solution extends the IOAM DEX Option-Type header with a Multicast Branch ID. Each branch fork node generates a unique ID for each branch and puts it in the header. The ID stays unchanged until the next fork node. For example, Node B might use [B, 0] for the branch to C and [B, 1] for the branch to D. Every node MUST export the received branch ID in its postcards, and with the Flow ID and Sequence Number the collector can rebuild the tree.

The ID has two parts: a 3-octet Branching Node ID and a two-octet Interface Index. It occupies 8 octets in total, and the three unused octets MUST be 0; otherwise the header is malformed and the packet MUST be dropped.

It is carried as an optional field after the Flow ID and Sequence Number. Two bits, N and I (the third and fourth bits of the Extension-Flags field), signal its presence. Two bits are used because RFC 9326 lets each extension flag cover only a 4-octet optional field. The two bits MUST be both set or both cleared, otherwise the header is malformed and the packet MUST be dropped.
sections.eli5: Each fork in the road hands out a name tag for each road, like Fork B Road 0. Every stop writes that tag on its note, so the notes can be sorted by road.

sections.title: Solution Two: Per-Section Postcard for IOAM Trace
sections.content:
The second solution combines the IOAM trace option (RFC 9197) with postcard-based telemetry. At each branch fork node, the trace data accumulated so far is exported as a postcard before the packet is replicated. The end node of each path also exports the final section as a postcard.

To let a collector correlate sections, each branch carries the fork node's own data, including its ID, in its trace. That data has to be carried per branch because each replicated copy can have different values, such as node delay, egress timestamp and egress interface. The postcard exported by the fork node itself can therefore hold only data common to all copies, such as ingress interface and ingress timestamp.

The IOAM trace option header format needs no change. Instead, branch fork nodes and leaf nodes are configured to export the trace so far and to refresh the IOAM header and data in the packet, for instance by clearing the node data list to all zeros and resetting the RemainingLen field to its initial value.
sections.eli5: At every fork, the traveller hands in the notes written so far and starts a clean page for each road. Every page begins with the fork's name, so the pages can be pieced together later.

sections.title: Fitting Into Multicast Protocols
sections.content:
The RFC discusses how the approach relates to existing multicast technology. Mtrace version 2 (RFC 8487) traces a multicast path by sending a Query to the Last-Hop Router, which is forwarded as a Request toward the source. The First-Hop Router turns it into a Reply. Mtrace2 does not integrate with IOAM directly, but network management systems may use it to learn which routers are of interest.

For PIM, the telemetry solution has to work within the multicast address ranges, 224.0.0.0 through 239.255.255.255 for IPv4 and ff00::/8 for IPv6, and cover UDP traffic. RFC 9486 describes a proposed way to carry the instruction header and metadata in IPv6. For multicast VPN, the RFC says IOAM and its recommendations apply equally to multicast MPLS packets (RFC 6514), and the telemetry must follow P2MP and MP2MP paths.
sections.eli5: The tracking idea has to work with the different ways multicast roads are built, including the ones inside private company networks.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The schemes share the security considerations of the IOAM trace option and the IOAM DEX option. Multicast already amplifies packets by nature, so the amplification risk of the DEX-based scheme is greater than for unicast, and stricter protections are needed.

Besides selecting which packets enable DEX and limiting the export rate, operators can allow only some nodes in the tree to process the option and export data. For example, only the branching nodes could be configured to do so.

IANA registered two Extension-Flags in the "IOAM DEX Extension-Flags" registry: bit 2, Multicast Branching Node ID, and bit 3, Multicast Branching Interface Index.
sections.eli5: Because one multicast packet becomes many copies, many notes could flood the collector. So only some stops should be asked to write notes.
